Let's see... I have built and sold thousands of these things.... I have a little advice for you.

Consider scraping up another half grand or so. There are a few extras you want to have if you are going to be gaming. You won't miss that extra money in year two or three, but you will still be pleased with the quality of your system, years after you bought it.

Computer technology is constantly improving. So it usually has a limited lifecycle, not in how long it lasts, but in how long it remains relevant. Buying the very newest stuff is dangerous, because it is unproven. Buying the cheapest stuff is foolish, because it becomes obsolete too fast, especially in the areas of games, and OS software updates. If you consider a scale of zero percent is the oldest, and 100% is the newest, what you want is to have a system built with hardware in the 50% to 75% range. It is still fairly new, but has also been around long enough to have customer reviews. When problems exist with specific parts, it always shows up in the customer reviews. It is easy to determine which parts to avoid, and which parts are the best value for your money.

If you are not building it yourself, have one of the better stores in town do it for you. Why? Local warranty coverage. If they build it, they will likely fix it if something goes wrong. If you buy the parts online, then it can be very difficult, frustrating, expensive, and time consuming, attempting to get any kind of repair. You may spend a lot of time without your system. Also, even though it might cost more dealing with the better store, it is also much more likely they will still be in business a couple of years down the road.

The thing with computer parts is this - if they are going to fail, they will usually do so very early on - like the first week or two. After that, you are usually good for a few years. Then normal wear and tear begins to show up and you again can find yourself in need of basic service. A well built computer can sometimes go ten years or more without needing anything - but it is also true that any single component can fail at any time. I do my own work, and still work with the stores, just because it is nice to have a local parts supplier who has everything I need, when I might need it. That's worth more than the money.

About that extra money - what should you buy with that?

A noise dampening case - best damned purchase I've ever made. My computer is quiet, and I sit right beside it. It has a whole bunch of fans and drives in there to make noise. A case like that costs about $50 more - worth every penny.

A bigger power supply - you may need some extra power down the road if you need to add more hardware, like new drives, or extra fans. If the system you are building now has a 550, then get the 650. Like that. Make sure there is a buffer.

A bigger screen with better quality. Can make a big difference in gaming, and it should serve you well for years. Check the reviews, then buy the better one you can still afford.

A better video card. Again, important for gaming. Again, check the reviews. Lean toward the newer models for software compatibility, but also the GPU and ram is generally the more the better when it comes to performance.

A decent gaming mouse. Makes a huge difference in gaming, but you also want one that fits your hand properly. Think ergonomics, a lot of gaming is a lot of opportunity for physical strain that leads to repetitive strain injury. The risk is very real and repetitive strain injury is nasty and can be crippling. A better mouse goes a long way in the right direction here.

Extra ram for the system: One of the more expensive purchases, and you want the better quality ram too. Tomorrow's applications always want more of it. I feel you are probably better off with a slower CPU and more ram, as versus the fastest CPU with not enough ram.

If there's any extra cash - consider a better sound system. You don't need top of the line, but stay away from the low end. Low end sound is just junk. Top end sound is a waste unless you are also buying sound cards. Mainboard built in sound is fine for gaming with a mid range system.

Headphones and mic - the cheap ones will hurt your ears, and crappy gear leads to com problems which will irritate your buddies online. Good gear is expensive, but worth it. Reviews again.

A decent computer chair (not part of this purchase - but you want one.)

I have found that these are not the areas most people think about when they buy a computer, but they become the areas they think about down the road after they have already made their purchase. I realize it seems extravagant, but it doesn't have to be. Take your time in your shopping, read the reviews, and plan out the system. You can cut small corners here and there and still build a well balanced package that covers these bases, coming in at about $1500. I got almost everything on that list for about $1200, but when I started some serious gaming, I needed the mouse, headphones and extra ram. That would have brought it up to $1500 or so. I ended up spending it anyways.

If your gaming computer lasts for five years, that's less than one dollar per day for a kick ass gaming platform. You are not going to miss the money. The quality is light years ahead of a base package.
